fixes.explanation: Sweet is the word. Moses cast the log into the waters, and “…they were sweetened.” (Exodus 15:25). The LORD was the one who showed him that log, so Moses didn't have to guess. After three days of walking without finding water, I think that was a big relief.

False is right. The LORD says, “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day.” (Exodus 16:4). Nobody is told to haul in a week's worth at once. The one change comes on the sixth day, when what they bring in is twice as much (Exodus 16:5).

Not the elders, friend. Moses says, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.” (Exodus 16:8). He points right past himself and Aaron and goes straight to the top. I think that's a man who knows exactly whose work this is.

A cloud. As Aaron is speaking, the people look toward the desert, “…and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared.” (Exodus 16:10). Aaron is mid-sentence, and the whole congregation is looking out at the desert. I bet that was one big turn of the head.

Quail. “That evening quail came and covered the camp…” (Exodus 16:13). Moses had said the LORD would give them meat that evening (Exodus 16:8), and the evening is when it shows up. Covered the camp, friend. I think that's a whole lot of birds.

Locusts would be a very different kind of visitor. The text says, “That evening quail came and covered the camp…” (Exodus 16:13). The LORD had told Moses that at twilight the people would eat meat (Exodus 16:12), and the quail are what arrived.

Nice try on the feathers, but it's a different bird. The text says, “That evening quail came and covered the camp…” (Exodus 16:13). Ravens never make an appearance in this scene. The bird on the scene is the quail, friend.

True. When they measured it by the omer, “…he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.” (Exodus 16:18). Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat. I think it's wonderful that the one who gathered little came up with no shortfall.

This one is false. Moses said, “No one may keep any of it until morning.” (Exodus 16:19). But the text says, “…they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning…” (Exodus 16:20). So it wasn't everyone leaving none of it. Moses was angry with them.

That's what happens. The leftover manna “…became infested with maggots and began to smell.” (Exodus 16:20). That was the part they kept after Moses said not to. I've forgotten a batch on the counter, but never one like that.
The text doesn't say anything about wind. It says the leftover manna “…became infested with maggots and began to smell.” (Exodus 16:20). What happened to it was maggots and a smell, not a breeze.

True. “So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots.” (Exodus 16:24). It's the same overnight wait as before, but a totally different result. Earlier, the leftovers had maggots and began to smell (Exodus 16:20).

Building isn't in this verse. The LORD says, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.” (Exodus 16:29). No construction crew, no big project, just staying put. Even a stamper with a mustache for hands can follow that one.

Years. “The Israelites ate manna forty years…” (Exodus 16:35), until they reached the border of Canaan. Forty years of the LORD's bread showing up for them. I can barely bake one more batch on a Monday, and they ate manna for forty years.
Forty weeks wouldn't even make it to a full year. The text says, “The Israelites ate manna forty years…” (Exodus 16:35). They kept eating it right up to the border of Canaan.
